The subantarctic landscape of Cape Froward National Park overlooks the Strait of Magellan. Eduardo Hernández Astudillo By Alexandra Gillespie Published October 20, 2026 Take Route 9 south from Punta Arenas along the Strait of Magellan until the road ends, then hike until you reach a 33-foot metal cross. This marks Cape Froward , the southernmost point in mainland South America, in a remote region where the Indigenous Kawésqar people have paddled the coast for 7,000 years , forests shelter endangered Andean deer, and bogs bank carbon by the ton. In 2027, the area will become Cape Froward National Park , the 19th and southernmost national stop on Patagonia’s 1,700-mile Route of Parks , a project led by the conservation nonprofit Rewilding Chile . Because there are no roads here, you’ll discover its raw wilderness on foot or by boat. ( See all 25 of the destinations that made our list of the best places to visit in 2027. ) When to Go Visit during the Southern Hemisphere's warm season, roughly October through April. If you’re lucky, you might even get to see one. Even if you don't, you’ll never be far from one, because this is bear country! Brown bears like the wide-open tundra while black bears prefer the forest, although they will sometimes venture out onto the tundra in search of food. Even though Kobuk Valley is in the Arctic, there are no polar bears here. Polar bears live on the sea ice and don't venture this far inland. Miller, Parker Lab/Caltech By Jason Bittel Published February 5, 2026 Life may look like a paradise for beetles living in ant colonies. Plump, wriggling ant larvae and helpless eggs sit waiting to be devoured, while hundreds of thousands of ants stand at the ready to ward off predators and parasites. There’s just one catch for these beetles, revealed in a new study published in the journal Cell . If one leaves the ant colony, it’ll be dead in less than a day. From bacteria living inside insect guts to mycorrhizal fungi on plant roots, symbiotic organisms abound across the tree of life, says Joseph Parker , an evolutionary biologist at the California Institute of Technology and senior author of the study. All these symbiotes have something in common that can also be a liability—their evolutionary entwinement has progressed so far, they can no longer live without their hosts. Parker and his colleagues wanted to know why. They tackled this question by investigating the odd relationship between a rove beetle known as Sceptobius lativentris and its host, the velvety tree ant. pages.description: The origin story has two settings: In Colorado, a gang of riders had the tenacity to conquer a treacherous terrain, and in California, others had the technology to design the ideal ride
pages.text: Before Mountain Biking Became One of the Most Popular Recreational Sports, Adventurous Souls of the American West Had to Invent a Rugged Bike Skip to main content Breeze’s earlier conceptual drawing for the Breezer 1 prototype. In the 1960s and ’70s, a countercultural movement drew a new generation of pioneers to the West. Suddenly, ski bums, scofflaws, draft dodgers and hippie homesteaders were joining the miners and hardscrabble farmers of mountain towns like Crested Butte, Colorado. Looking for a way to navigate both the Pontiac-bedeviling potholes in town as well as the dirt roads leading into the mountains, a small crew of Crested Butte transplants began building handmade off-road-ready bikes. They used a hodgepodge of vintage parts, in particular from World War II-era Schwinn bicycles. The group called itself the Grubstake Gang (named after a favorite watering hole), and they rejoiced when their heavy cruisers, outfitted with fat tires, proved capable of handling the punishing unpaved roads into and out of town. In September 1976, 15 cyclists attempted a seemingly impossible feat: riding these “klunkers” over 12,700-foot Pearl Pass to Aspen. The next day, just two riders rolled into Aspen; the steep Colorado stones of the 38-mile road had destroyed all the other klunkers. Around the same time, a group of teenagers in California’s Marin County—they called themselves the Larkspur Canyon Gang —were tinkering and racing their own garage-built bikes down the steep roads of Mount Tamalpais , north of San Francisco. pages.description: Discover the fascinating origins of many of our beloved nursery rhymes with the British Library's newly acquired rare and early edition of Mother Goose's Melody.
pages.text: Before they were bedtime stories Skip to content Collection What's on Visit Stories About us Contact and help Opening hours Everything for Research Business Schools Family Support us Shop Search our main catalogue Before they were bedtime stories: the first printed nursery rhymes The British Library has acquired Mother Goose's Melody, a rare and early edition of British nursery rhymes. Read on to discover more about this little book and the fascinating origins of many of our beloved nursery rhymes. 13 November 2026 Blog series English and Drama Author Maddy Smith, Lead Curator of Printed Heritage Collections (1601-1900) Have you ever wondered where nursery rhymes like 'hush-a-bye baby', 'hickery dickery dock', 'baa baa black sheep' and 'Jack and Gill went up the hill' came from? Well, it's World Nursery Rhyme Week and the British Library has recently acquired for the nation an exceptionally rare copy of Mother Goose's Melody: or, Sonnets for the Cradle printed in 1791. This is a little children's book full of rhymes, humour and entertaining woodcut illustrations, and it contains the first recorded appearance in print of many nursery rhymes still familiar to us today. It is one of the most important collections of nursery rhymes ever published in Britain. Many later editions of traditional nursery rhymes in Britain and North America were based on rhymes in Mother Goose's Melody. Even Arkansans have largely forgotten that this attractive spa town was America’s original Sin City, teeming with casinos and brothels, and frequented by big-name gangsters. The mobster Bugsy Siegel may have even used Hot Springs as an inspiration when he was developing the Las Vegas Strip. The leading authority on the town’s colorful, decadent, sinful history (it was known as “the loose buckle in the Bible Belt”) is a charismatic, white-haired, sharp-dressed man named Robert K. Raines. pages.text: Ben Franklin Wasn’t Serious When He Implied the Wild Turkey Would Be a ‘Respectable’ National Symbol … but He Wasn’t Wrong, Either Skip to main content The head of a male turkey is distinguished by the colorful dewlap and caruncles on its neck. Joanna Lentini The wild turkey is a noble beast: the muscular, bronze-sheened ancestor of the barnyard turkeys we eat today. While the two technically belong to the same species, the barnyard variety is relatively new on the scene. People began domesticating wild turkeys in what is now Mexico more than 2,000 years ago, selectively breeding them over generations to become fat and docile. Wild turkeys, meanwhile, have inhabited North America for a much longer time—hundreds of thousands of years. Hunters still eat them, of course, and appreciate the lean gaminess of the wild flesh. But for most of us, the bird is less about sustenance than about a glimpse of the true national temperament: resourceful and restless, by turns noble and idiotic—as liable to swagger into view as to bolt for the trees. This feathery American character has long invited comparison with another native bird. When the Continental Congress first chose the bald eagle for our fledgling nation’s heraldry, Benjamin Franklin wrote to his daughter in 1784 condemning it as “a bird of bad moral character,” given to stealing food from smaller birds rather than hunting for itself. The topic is considered at greater detail in a separate technical note .) SQLite has been used with great success as the on-disk file format for desktop applications such as version control systems, financial analysis tools, media cataloging and editing suites, CAD packages, record keeping programs, and so forth. The traditional File/Open operation calls sqlite3_open() to attach to the database file.
